sections.h:
Reasons for thanking the Lord for the divine mercies granted in 1879: the Church's recognition of the Family of Saint Anne; the foundation of new Houses, also in America; the service to the poor of Piacenza; the considerable number of vocations: 57 sisters received the habit, a number reduced by the hardship of the times, since the Mother House could not receive young women without a dowry. Recommendations to Superiors and Sisters. Notice of the deceased Sisters to be prayed for.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughters,

  1. Our Institute, the family of the August and glorious Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate our Mother, has now entered the fourteenth year of its existence, a year we hope will be one of great glory for it, as was the year just ended.

  2. Yes, Daughters, very many are the divine mercies with which the year 1879 was filled. The greatest, most heartfelt and splendid is that Holy Church, through her Vicar, now Leo XIII, has definitively recognised our family as a Religious family, which is to say a family of God.1

  3. This approval was welcomed, since it leaves not the slightest doubt that those who gather in it find all the means to reach that eminent holiness to which God calls those who make special profession of the evangelical counsels of poverty, obedience and chastity.2

  4. As a result we see the peoples' sympathy ever growing towards us, who bear the most noble name of Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, and so we are certain that this name, the most

honourable for a creature, we did not take for ourselves, but it was imposed on us by heaven.3

  1. A clear sign of this sympathy is the many requests received for founding houses in various places. The foundations agreed number 19, nine of which have already opened and the other ten will open shortly.4 Among these new houses one has been founded in America, in Bolivia, beside the one already there.5 In it some 80 girls of ours are being educated in religion. Negotiations are under way to found, likewise there in America, three more houses in three different cities,6 to which 40 Sisters would be called.

  2. This eagerness to have our Sisters arises from seeing the fine results obtained by the peoples who have them, both in hospitals and in schools.

  3. One of the benefits the Lord is pleased to bestow on His creatures through our Sisters, and which deserves special mention, is the distribution of soup to the poor. In this winter of seventy-nine and eighty the Lord is punishing the sins of the world with cold and hunger.7 Well, His mercy, which is never separated from His divine justice, has called us, His ministers, to relieve so many wretched people, giving them food and clothing every day. In the Mother House alone some three thousand beggars are fed daily with good, well-seasoned soup.8

  4. What a great grace this is, Sisters! What a sign of predilection the Lord gives us! The way to thank Him for such distinction is to humble ourselves before His divine Majesty, sincerely acknowledging our unworthiness, and to work unsparingly to carry out so noble an office.

  5. The number clothed was 57, far fewer than in '78; but the reason was not a shortage of postulants asking to wear the habit of the Holy Mother; it was that, in these critical times, they could not bring the required dowry, small as it is. On the other hand the Mother House, given the hardship of the times, could not open its arms to receive them without a dowry.

  1. And here we must urge thrift, especially on the Superiors, so that after feeding and clothing the Sisters they can send any surplus to the Mother House.

  2. They are bound to this by love, by vow and by justice. By love: they must know that the fruitfulness of the Institute

depends on two things: the first is that the Lord call many, even with a very small dowry or none. Now this year the first was not lacking, for the requests were very many, but the Mother House lacked the means to receive them without a dowry. And on whom does it depend that the Mother House has these means? It depends precisely on the thrift of the Superiors.

  1. It is consoling to say that many true Daughters of the Holy Mother, eager to see her family spread throughout the world, are most careful to account for every penny, as the saying goes, so as to have surplus to send to the Mother House, knowing that the well-being of the whole Institute springs from its well-being.9 The Mother House is the heart of the Institute; if the heart is healthy and full of life, the members in the other Houses are also healthy and strong.

  2. But the Holy Mother does not receive this joy from all. There are some spendthrifts who, despite generous allowances, never have anything to save. They are unloving and unnatural, caring nothing for the Institute's glory. Besides not10 being unloving towards the Institute, they risk failing in justice by harming it, for let them remember that they are not owners of the goods of the Houses they head, but simply administrators.

  3. It is worth noting that, just as Superiors who love the Institute and take care not to squander its goods also treat their sisters well, loving them when healthy and caring for them when sick, so those who live only for themselves and cannot save neglect their sisters and make them go short of food and clothing.

  4. We must also again impress on some Superiors that they should beware of fearing that the sisters will write to the Mother about them: this fear springs from duplicity, for simple-hearted Superiors like to be known by their Mother so as to be helped to advance in virtue and free themselves of faults.

  5. But these Superiors say: "We do not mind people writing to the Mother about our doings, but we do mind their writing falsehoods and slander". A frivolous pretext, dictated by their pride and arrogance. Humility loves to resemble Jesus Christ, who for love of us chose to submit to being slandered. This pretext, moreover, wrongs the [higher] Superiors, treating them as imprudent and rash, unable to weigh the reports they receive against Superiors so as to tell the false from the true.11

  6. And if now and then the Lord permits Superiors to be deceived, this serves to bring out all the more the innocence of the one slandered, and afterwards the Lord uses her to do great good for His glory.

  7. A Superior who fears and resents the sisters writing to the Mother is utterly unworthy of being one, and once the Superiors discover this base and dishonourable sin in her, she must be inexorably removed from office.

  8. Let us now consider the sisters' duty towards their Superiors. The sisters must have eyes to see their Superiors' wishes, to receive them reverently and carry them out promptly, to see the duty of the office laid on them, whether as nurse or in school, etc., etc., and fulfil it faithfully; but they must be blind so as not to pry into and investigate their Superiors' conduct.

  9. Here perhaps the difficulty will arise in their minds: "but the rule does require the sisters to inform the Mother of serious faults in their superiors". How can we fulfil this duty if we do not observe them?

  10. Sisters, Superiors are like the sun, which, being on high, cannot hide its large spots that eclipse it from anyone not wholly without eyes. So it is with the grave faults of Superiors that ruin their souls and scandalise their subjects; these faults are necessarily seen by the sisters even with their eyes closed.

  11. All see if she wickedly goes out of her way to speak alone with persons of the other sex; all see if through lukewarmness she neglects works of piety; all see if she does not follow the Mother House in providing her Community with food and clothing, or if she is not a mother to the sick. So let the sisters love their Superiors with a sincere love, a filial love, a love that is reverent, humble and obedient, and then they will always find them good.

  12. We end this letter by noting the number of sisters the Holy Mother added to her crown last year. I mean those fortunate sisters who have reached the one supreme end for which they joined the Institute, which is to die the death of the just, the death precious in God's sight, a death that has nothing fearful but its name; for in reality it is only a passage from misery to happiness, from suffering to en-

joyment, from humiliation to eternal glory. These favoured ones numbered 15. The sisters are asked for the customary prayers for the dead. Urging you, dearest daughters, to profit by these counsels, we implore the Lord's Blessing upon you, and remain in the sacred hearts of Jesus and Mary and of the Holy Mother your affectionate

Giov. Batta. Tornatore Miss. M. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The related letters announcing it to the communities and the Bishops are given in Lettere 5, nos. 288 and 290.

2 The approval was welcomed because it gives all who join the certainty that in it they find every means to attain the particular holiness to which God calls them, professing according to the Rule the evangelical counsels of poverty, obedience and chastity.

3 // name of daughters of Saint Anne... imposed on us by heaven: The Rule of 1869, Ch. 1, no. 1 reads: "God calls you to my Family, that you may imitate me; that you may be most splendid copies of me, Mother of the Immaculate. This work must be the work of Divine Love... so that you may be my daughters".

4 For the houses opened in 1879 cf. Lettere 4, index IV; for the rest, this vol., index IV.

5 This is the "Saint Anne School" in La Paz.

6 In three different cities: Potosí, Tarija, Sucre.

7 The Mother speaks of this in several letters published here.

8 Mother Rosa specifies the number of people helped and the places. Cf. L 13,2

9 The Mother House was the administrative centre of the Family.

10 ... besides not: besides being

11 ...wrongs the Superiors: it speaks ill of the major Superiors, implying that they are imprudent and rash and cannot properly weigh the reports reaching them against local Superiors so as to tell true from false.

The Superior for the new house at Pisa will arrive. Let her accompany her and organise everything, instructing her and the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, you will receive this letter from Sr. A. Ancilla; she is coming to be Superior at Pisa, where on Thursday you will telegraph the Parish Priest and tell him the time of your arrival.1 He writes that I should first send two to organise the House.

  2. So I have thought of doing this: you will go with her and when everything is in order you will telegraph me to send the others. As for the others, for the money tell the Parish Priest that when I have sent them I will send him the whole account, so he will see what has been spent.2

  3. Stay until they are well settled; I urge you to instruct her well, teach her, and you will be able to tell me whether she is good and doing well;3 likewise Sr. A. Cipriana, who comes with her; she is one of those going to Pisa, an angel in the flesh, and meanwhile, staying in Pistoia, she will go a little to the sick and learn to pull teeth, which I am sure she will do very well. Tell me something as soon as you are in that house. Do you understand? Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior is Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli. She will accompany her, giving the Parish Priest advance notice.

2 The travel expenses.

3 Whether she is doing well refers to the Superior.

She is glad of the good news of the Community. She asks for a Sister for a few days. Two others will come to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am glad of what you tell me about the Sisters; truly I can say it is my only consolation when I hear that all is well and the Sisters are behaving well.

  2. Now I would really like you to do me the kindness of lending me Sr. A. Reparata for a few days;1 I have to open a hospital and would need her by Thursday; I hope she will be here, won't she?2 And I will send you Sr. A. Sabina with another one provisionally, and then return Reparata to you. So do me this favour. On Thursday I will expect her on the 2 p.m. train, and that same day I will send you the other two. Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Reparata Fabrini. 2 Thursday, 5 February.

She sends the receipt for the shipment of the case. Letters are not arriving; she sends this L by registered post. She hopes order and peace will be restored under the new President. She explains how to send the payment for the cloth she bought and sent. Various news from Piacenza and a request for news. She will send the circular letter at the end of the month.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

  1. I received your letter dated 3 November on 31 January 1880. I hear you never receive the case and would like to know the name of the steamer; I am sending you the insurance document, you will see everything;1 I have already sent you another registered letter and you never acknowledge receipt. I do not know what to think; I always send you everything registered and never see that you receive it. Let us hope you will.

  2. I hope it is all over, for I hear they have made another president, is it true?2 How I have suffered! Enough, I look forward to your telling me about it. Because of this I hope there will be no more revolution, for surely everything will have been settled.

  3. As for the rest, for sending me what you mention,3 Gaspare had written to you how to do it, but I see you never receive these blessed letters, which would be the safest way; then I could pay for the cloth I sent you; not wanting to wait any longer, I had to pay for ours, which came to a fine sum, and yours is 1600 f,4 plus shipping costs; so enclosed you will find again the person to whom you should hand them, a banker who then remits them by draft to this one in Piacenza, and then we get them at once; that is how you should do it.

  4. I hear about Sr. A. Clelia. If you thought her capable, she could come back saying she is coming to fetch the others, and then I would send another; what do you think?5 Do as you think best, and the Lord will see to it, for surely the Holy Mother will not allow her to go her own way; she will set her right!

  5. So one of you must come sooner or later, for I hear you are taking postulants, and when you have 8 or 10 who have done 6 or 8 months of novitiate they will have to come here; that way you will have more room to make some changes; what do you think?

  6. I would like to hear that you are a little stronger and sturdier and back to how you were, in short, robust.6 It is very cold here and, worse, there is great hunger. If you saw how many soups are given out you would not believe it.7 At Cortemaggiore too they give out as many.

  7. For two days there has been a little sun and the cold is easing. I am still in Piacenza and cannot leave until the end of February because I have an immense amount to do. I hope that before you receive this you will have received all the others, including the registered ones.

  8. At the end of this month I will send you the circular we are printing;8 I have also written to all the sisters, and in one of yours, which could not be properly understood, you seemed to say that Sr. A. Lucia has died, is it true? I do not know how to take it, you tell me nothing;9 I also wrote to Father Rocchi and to the Bishop [by] the other post.

  9. I hope the war will end and then letters will no longer go astray, for from what I see a good number have been lost; clearly there is confusion, but what grieves me most is the big case of cloth that has gone missing. Let us hope not! I would like you to write to me as soon as you receive this. Oh! if a telegram did not cost so much, how gladly I would receive one! Enough. You will do what you think best.

  1. Now let us talk a little about observance, and let us hope it always flourishes in America as, by God's mercy, it does in this House and in all those of Upper and Lower Italy.10 From the circular you will see the faults that prevail in the houses, especially that of disposing of the Institute's goods and taking the liberty of giving them to relatives, and likewise the letters they write; enough, you will read it.

  2. I hope the Sisters have settled down well and that peace reigns. I have also written to Sr. A. Rosa.11 In this one I am not writing to any-

one; in another I will answer all the sisters who write to me. Goodbye, yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

1 She sends the receipt for the shipment of the case of cloth.

2 Another President. Cf. L 21, n. 9

3 What you mention: the payment for the cloth sent to her.

4 Cf. L 21, n. 8.

5 Sr. A. Clelia Semeria. One of the daughters of the benefactor Benigno Clavijo had formed a strong friendship with her and often wanted to be with the Sister. Rumours had arisen. The Bishop too wanted to get to the bottom of it through a canonical visitation of the Sisters' community, questioning them individually. Cf. L to M. Rosa: 20.11.'80 from Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni and 1880 letters from Sr. A. Clelia to M. Rosa.

6 Cf. L 21, n. 1.

7 Cf. L 13,2.

8 This is L 24.

9 Sr. A. Lucia Taraballi had died in October 1879. Cf. L to M. Rosa: 16.10.'79 from Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni.

10 Observance, i.e. the life of fidelity to vocation and mission instilled by the Foundress. In urging it on the Superior, the Mother can state that it prevails in the Mother House and in all the Houses of northern and southern Italy.

11 Cf. L 7, n. 8.

She consoles her on her brother's sudden death. May prayer and reflection help her benefit the soul of the deceased and find peace herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear of your grief with great sorrow,1 but you must reflect that we are made for this end, and besides, a dear daughter of Saint Anne must think of praying and of being able to help that soul.2

  2. Oh! daughter, think that in your position you can help him with holy resignation and prayers, Holy Communion, Mass every day. How could my daughter, so gifted with intelligence, let herself be cast down by such useless sadness?3 Reason, time and reflection are the only things that bring peace.

  3. Sure that my daughter will do so, I hold you close in the heart of Jesus, where I hope you will find everything, including peace, and be content; and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Overwhelmed with grief, she had told her that same day of the sudden death of her 16-year-old brother.

2 Reflection and prayer are the means that help one not to sink into unspeakable sorrow.

3 Sr. A. Agnese had described her state of mind: "I am turned to stone... I can find no relief".

Her letters have not arrived; she has sent several, some registered. She suggests how and what to say to the Sisters about her instructions and admonitions. They need gentleness. She urges her to write to the Bishop of Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You want letters and tell me that for several days you have received none; they must have gone astray; besides, I have sent you several by registered post, especially those containing the receipts for the case, and I sent another registered one about 8 days ago. Now I keep a record of them1 and I assure you I always write, I never miss a post.

  2. Listen, would it not be good if in the chapters2 you hold, speaking gently and kindly, you said: "Daughters, do not be scandalised if you see me give something extra or make some difference for someone;3 do not think I love her more! No, to me you are all my dearest sisters, and I assure you that if at times I urge you to take courage and not fear evil so much, it is because I know the ground I am testing is good, and by sometimes going deep to the roots4 the virtues stand out all the more. For the rest, bear with me too in many things if you find me too stern; but I assure you that one day you will see that my firmness was only to make you grow in virtue".

  3. Believe me, daughter, our dear daughters are children and also need a little petting.5

For pity's sake, let favouritism never enter your community, for it would be the plague. But knowing you well enough, I know how fair you are; I do not doubt this at all.

4. Write, I repeat, to the Bishop here in Piacenza; you should have done so before, for it really would have been your duty.

For now I add nothing; I would only like to hear that you are strong, robust and healed of your infirmities,5 while I call myself yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The irregular arrival of letters worried them both. Cf. L 7.1,5; 21.1,5; 27,1,3-

2 Community meetings.

3 Something extra..., in the food given to Sisters who need it.

4 going deep to the roots: exposing the hidden origins of wrong behaviour.

5 Expressions full of humanity and motherly tenderness.

6 Cf. L 21.1.

She praises her for starting the new house at Pisa. She awaits more consoling news.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. Your letter was a real consolation amid countless sorrows!2 well done, well done; may God continue to give you His holy light and you to respond to it.

  2. So the Pisa house is open; now we must see to consolidating it. Well, now it is up to you to see that instead of 4, who are no use at all,3 there are at least 6 or 8; it seems to me that with the salary they have they can manage very well, and I will send the alms-collectors,4 for I have two really good ones.

  3. I await your letters; write to me often, for they are a real consolation. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 This date is assumed from the content and from Sr. A. Crocifissa's correspondence. Cf. letters of February 1880.

2 Amid countless sorrows. Crosses were never lacking, starting with her poor health.

3 Four Sisters would have been of no use, since there were many requests for home nursing.

4 The Sisters would obtain from alms-collecting some help towards their keep.

She shares her grief and invites her to resignation and prayer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I share as much as I can and know all your grief, but! one thing holds me back, and that is holy resignation!2 Listen, my dear daughter, I have been through all these sorrows and more: my son! and a father, a brother, but! resigned! and only in holy resignation

did I find comfort.3

2. I threw myself into the heart of Jesus, I had recourse to the Crucified, and in Him, my dear, oh! I always found everything.4

Try it and you will see.5 I leave you in the heart of Jesus6 and call myself

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The letter, written from Piacenza, is dated 7.4.80, but it is certainly from February, as the context of the correspondence and the established facts of this

period show. Cf. L 28.

2 I share... resignation. In her L of 6.2.'80 Sr. A. Agnese had explained the details of her brother's death; he was accidentally killed by a cousin during a hunting party.

3 Faced with the forces of evil and sorrow she finds comfort in faith, entrusting herself to the God of life.

4 In the heart of Jesus... I found everything. Not only did she draw consolation and strength.

5 In the Crucified the awareness of the saving meaning of suffering was illuminated.

6 The Sister replied on 9.2.80 that she had experienced the effectiveness of her advice.

Advice. She urges her to be cheerful.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear of your troubles and make them mine; send the girl away at once, for one can spoil all the others. Have her accompanied by the two alms-collectors or by others you think fit.1

  2. I understood little of your letter;2 I only tell you to keep your spirits up and be cheerful; after the storm comes fair weather.

Goodbye, thank you for the basket3

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 One of the girls of the Institute had run away and the anxious Superior had searched for her in vain. She told the Mother, saying she was determined to send the runaway home. The Mother supports her and suggests having her accompanied by the two Sisters who go collecting alms, or by others. After questioning the girl the Superior decided to keep her. Cf. her letters to M. Rosa; 4.2 and 7.2.1880.

2 The Superior had hinted at difficulties in the house without being specific.

3 She had sent her the gift of the poor: "two cabbage tops from the garden and chickpea flour". Cf. L 26.1.1880 to M. Rosa.

She tells her of her coming departure. She asks for prayers.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. I received yours with the statement enclosed,1 and so I hear the many good items of news. God willing, at the end of this [month] I shall leave Piacenza. I do not know when I shall reach Rome, because I must stop in many places.2 Pray and have others pray that I may have a good journey, and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The statement of accounts.

2 She left Piacenza on 28.2. Cf. L 34, n. 2. She visited the houses of Pistoia, Pisa, Florence and Montalto di Castro.

She informs her of her coming departure from Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. God willing, next Wednesday2 I shall set out, but first I have to visit two houses and then I will go to Pistoia; I will telegraph you before leaving the last house.

  2. You have done everything well; I approve it all.3 We shall talk better in person. Goodbye, I am your

affectionate M. Rosa

I greet everyone and am

1 The date is inferred from the context and in particular from Sr. A. Crocifissa's reply of 22.2.'80 to this L.

2 Wednesday 25 February; in fact she left the following Saturday, the 28th. Cf. L 38, n. 3.

3 This refers to the organisation of the Pisa house. Cf. the related correspondence of Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi.

She gives her opinion on accepting a postulant.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. I have received a letter from a certain Diega Corso of your Orphanage, who would like to be accepted among the Daughters of Saint Anne. If you think she is truly good like the other one I accepted, tell her she is accepted like the other.

  2. See that they have at least the fare for the journey1 and then you will bring her to me in Naples with the other. Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The postulants were orphans and lacked the dowry normally required.

She explains how to overcome her doubts about confession and what principles to follow to benefit from it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am so busy that I do not know how to answer your letter.1 I will only tell you that we must hold firmly to [what] Holy Mother Church has taught us: that to make a good and holy confession we must aim at nothing but intense sorrow for our sins and earnest resolutions to amend, and look at nothing else.

  2. If you do this, be sure you will be dear to the heart of Jesus, in the lively hope of amending all your faults, making earnest promises never to fall back, keeping the Holy Rules and asking God for holy perseverance. Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me always

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Sister had written revealing her doubts and anxieties about confession and asking for spiritual comfort and consolation.

She authorises the work on the house. She has received the money order.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Courage, then, and never mistrust that dear Jesus who does everything for our good. I have written to Cimatti to go ahead with certain works.1 I received the money order and have already handed everything over; if you can, send the rest; if not, I will make it up.2 You ought to send me something of the half-year accounts3 of that house. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She authorised the master builder Cimatti to carry out the work.

2 She received the money order for £ 60, an advance on the cloth the Mother had bought for her; she will complete the payment. But the Mother reassures her: send the rest if possible, otherwise she will settle it all herself.

3 // half-year: the accounts for the second half of 1879.

Alarmed at what she has written about the Superior of the Pisa house, she proposes two solutions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your letter1 and hear that you have already begun the nursing, but the news of that sister who was to be superior — this way she behaves — hurts me deeply;2 so, since Jesus has let us know her, we must at once try to put it right.

  2. This is what we will do: send her to Pistoia and bring Sr. A. Geronima, whom you left in your place, to you, and make her vice-superior; then you can go straight to Pistoia and put your little affairs in order, and I will not be long in coming, for God willing I shall leave next Saturday,3 but I must stop at two houses and then I shall be with you, for I see the sisters have little affection for this superior.4

  3. If, however, you think she could continue, then we will do this: read her these two lines I put at the foot of this letter; you must leave her as vice-superior. She will be able to do nothing without your consent, and you will go there every month, receive the alms-collectors' money and leave her only what is strictly necessary, and she will be vice-superior.5

  4. Meanwhile I am writing to her, so she will calm down, and the sisters too, and everything will be settled.

Tomorrow, God willing, I hope to send you two sisters. Goodbye; much more in person

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The L is dated 22 February 1880.

2 The sister appointed Superior, Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli, had asked Superior Crocifissa for a new habit and "a nice wallet". This alarmed M. Rosa.

3 Saturday 28 February.

4 She went to Lugo; cf. L 47,9; and to Ferrara; cf. letters from Sr. A. Eufrasina Pizzoni to M. Rosa n.d. and 10.3.'80. For this Superior: Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli. Cf. L 39.

5 She will be vice-Superior and so have a good training under Sr. A. Crocifissa, who by now had much experience.

She reassures her by relieving her of the office of Superior pending her visit, now imminent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I gather from your letter that you are not very happy;1 well then, we will do this: provisionally, until I arrive, you will remain vice-superior and Sr. A. Crocifissa Superior, and when she goes to Pisa2 you will take her orders and abide by what she tells you. Be cheerful, for in a few days I shall be there. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She was not only inexperienced but also too timid.

2 Sr. A. Crocifissa is Superior of the Pistoia House, and when she has to go to Pisa you will follow her orders. Cf. L 25; 34; 38.

She appoints her Superior and explains how she should handle the administration. She will send her a Sister teacher as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. So, pay close attention: in the name of my beloved Jesus, listen to me, act, and obey exactly. This is what we will do: you will remain Superior, and when you go collecting alms Sr. A. Colomba will take your place,1 and I hope you will do well and I shall have no cause for sorrow.

  2. Now to financial matters: I will send you all the books,2 where you will see what you must collect and the money I hold.

  3. As for the teaching certificate, I will do everything to prevent a little lay teacher being brought in too soon,3 but for the moment I do not know what to do; meanwhile you have a certificate there and can say so; you must send it by registered post with 5 seals to Invorio Inferiore at once, and I will do everything to send you another.4

  4. I assure you I am very, very anxious, but I hope you will be well and find a way out. I really do not know whom to send you for the alms-collecting; enough, let us hope.5

Goodbye, your affectionate. Do not come yourself, for it would be useless. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. As for the girl for service, the Count does not want her, so you need not send her to be trained; there is no need for her to go.6

1 The superior, Sr. A. Genoveffa Molinari, had been transferred a few days earlier. Now the Mother appoints Sr. A. Costanza.

2 She will send her the account books. The Mother had taken them with her a few days earlier when visiting the community.

3 The little orphans received elementary education within the Institute. To avoid the immediate hiring of a lay teacher, the Mother will do her best to assign a qualified sister to the Lodi House.

4 ...you have... another. For the moment you can say you have a certificate, but remember that you must send it to Invorio Inferiore, since it belongs to the Sister recently transferred there.

5 A Sister was needed for alms-collecting to spare the Superior this task, incompatible with her role, which required her constant presence in the house.

She thanks her and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Thank you for what you do for me;2 as for doubting that the Most Holy Virgin will grant me the grace — oh! that is too much! Enough, pray and have others pray! Thank you for the potatoes. As for the Postulants, do as you say.

Goodbye, yours in my dear Crucified One

affectionate M. Rosa

By the end of next week I shall be in Florence.

1 From the context it can be assigned to this period.

2 Aware of the Mother House's needs, she sent part of what was given to the alms-collecting Sisters: cheese, wool, oil, wheat, etc.

She orders her to leave at once for Pisa, where Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting to instruct her about the house and the work.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. As soon as you receive this letter, without saying anything to anyone, anyone at all, take your things and leave for Pisa, where Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting for you and will install you as Superior of that house.2

  2. I repeat, say nothing to anyone and leave right away for Pisa, because that Superior3 has been removed to open a new house.

  3. You are changing for the better: first, you will be closer to Rome and we shall be able to see each other more often; second, because it is a lovely little house and you will be very, very happy there.

  4. So we are agreed; go at once, at once, for Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting for you and will instruct you in everything and tell you how to proceed. In the firm confidence that you will obey blindly, holding you close to my dear Crucified One, I call myself yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa G.

Please leave at once without objections.

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Sr. A. Antonietta was at Ferrara: cf. letters to M. Rosa: 14.2 and 27.2.'80 from Sr. A. Agnese Sismondini.

3 Leave for Pisa because the Superior of that house, Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli, had been assigned elsewhere.

She urges observance of the Rules: let her put an end to grumbling and to listening to insinuations. She clarifies the scope of her task.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I read your two letters just as I arrived from Pistoia,2 after suffering horribly, but always gladly, for I know that suffering alone is good for my soul. So you flee from it! and you are my daughter! it cannot be! the most beautiful and sweet comfort is loving Jesus!

  2. Oh! ill-starred tongues that fall upon your papier-mâché heart, sacrilegious grumblings and, worse still, diabolical vipers.3 What good have the Father's sermons done?4 You tell me: either she goes or I go; why such fury?5 Oh! you say you love a poor Mother, but what can I say? I must say I do not believe it.

  3. Let me give vent to my thoughts, for if that were so it seems to me you should not act like this; first you would keep our holy Rules by putting an end to grumbling — first by not listening to it at all, so as to set an example to the others; besides, you would not feel your heart wounded by muddled6 words reported to you, for whoever speaks in passion never tells the truth.

  4. So you must realise that as soon as you mention to the Mother the girls and anything that is wrong, which you see with your own eyes, she will certainly not be slow to remedy it; but these are not rifle shots!7

  5. As for her, I tell you she should have little or nothing to do with you; it is enough that she does not prevent you from doing your job and treats you well; otherwise there is nothing to be done.8

  6. I cannot understand, regarding the linen, if it happened that she gave you others' linen, which I do not believe, for you will see for yourself.9

  7. Listen, in two months I shall be back and will come; your wish will be granted; meanwhile look after yourself, for pity's sake.

  8. Accepting the girls depends on the superior, but that one is an illegitimate child who can be accepted, for she is not one of those who count among the foundlings.10 Goodbye, I am unwell and find it hard to write.

Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 In April the Mother was not in Pistoia. From the text of this letter and of the two it answers, it is from March.

2 The two letters: of 7 and 9 March 1880.

3 Oh! ill-starred tongues... diabolical. A strong rebuke in a satirical tone and heavily negative figurative language.

4 The sermons and exhortations of Fr Tornatore.

5 Either she goes or I go. She is the superior Eufrosina Pizzoni, whom the Mother had taken to Ferrara to relieve Sr. A. Agnese of the burden of being superior; Sr. Agnese had complained several times, begging the Mother to let her devote herself only to the boarders and the College. After the superior's arrival, however, she changed her mind and wrote the Mother a letter of strong complaint against the Superior.

6 Muddled: incoherent, untrue.

7 ...as soon as... rifle shots. When you tell me about the girls and what is wrong, which you have seen for yourself, I shall certainly not be slow to remedy it. But do not demand immediate action even then (they are not rifle shots).

8 As for her (the Superior)... done. She clarifies the respective roles of the Superior and the Director of the College.

9 The Sister had written that the Superior had given her linen to the others and she feared she would have to receive linen not her own.

10 She had written word for word: "that girl of good family who was to come in, I have learnt that she is a foundling". The Mother clarifies: she can be accepted because she was adopted.

An alms-collecting Sister must be transferred to Piacenza. Let her see to it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1, I hear with no little surprise what happened to the two alms-collectors;1 so this cannot be all; other consequences would follow.2

2. So it is time to take her away from Genoa; send her to Piacenza at once, and you can go collecting yourself; and God willing, on my return from Rome I will come and then we can...3

Enough, I am overwhelmed with work,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 There is no information on what had happened to the sisters who went collecting alms.

2 What had happened could not be considered an isolated case; other negative consequences would follow.

3 ... and then we can decide how else to replace the Sister.

She tells her to send two Sisters to Ferrara, with the relevant explanations.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. Listen, I need you to send Sr. A. Ulderica to Ferrara at once, provisionally, with the alms-collector who will have arrived from Sestri, called Sr. A. Ferdinanda? If she has not arrived, then let Sr. A. Gabriella go with Sr. A. Ulderica, and send them to Ferrara on the 1.40 through train; one obedience paper made out to Ferrara is enough.3 At once, at once, because I need them to be in Ferrara tomorrow evening.

  2. I am not continuing in my own hand because I must go out, and tomorrow I leave for Florence;4 I will expect letters there.

The Lord bless you,

most affectionate Mother Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

P.S. Tell them that as soon as they reach Bologna they should look for the Ferrara train straight away.

  • Send some large sacks here at once to be filled with chestnuts and potatoes.

  • Sr. A. Gabriella does not need a bundle,5 the others do.

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Francesca's L of 14.3.1880 replying to M. Rosa.

2 Sr. A. Ferdinanda had arrived in Piacenza on 4.3.'80. Sr. A. Francesca had informed the Mother.

3 The obedience paper: the name given to the railway fare-reduction voucher.

4 The L was completed by Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega.

5 bundle, the bag or small sack with personal linen.

She announces the arrival of the new Superior and her own.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. When Sr. A. Antonietta1 arrives, do not say anything to her about her being Superior. Wait for me first; when I come we will do everything.

  2. Today I expected letters from you telling me something about the house there.2

Goodbye; on Sunday [I shall leave] on the 5 p.m. train and arrive at half past 7. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Antonietta Gallinari was arriving from Ferrara. Cf. L 42, n. 2.

2 The Pisa house, where she had gone to start up and organise home nursing. Cf. L 25.

She praises her obedience, the virtue that leads to the perfection of love. She urges her to love, pray and act only out of love, accepting suffering. She gives her various tasks. Advice. News.

A.M.E

Dearest daughter,

  1. Your telegram was a real consolation to me, showing your obedience. Oh! blessed are you if you know how to practise this beautiful virtue well; it is the only one that serves us to advance on the way of perfection and obtain the love of God!2

  2. Dear Francesca, this alone can be the delight and contentment of your heart; this is our only sure, unchanging, eternal good; all the rest is deceptive, perishable and fleeting.

  3. You alone, my Good, are the unchanging one, the only good that can make our love happy.3

  4. Yes, my dear daughter, love, love Jesus alone! May the dear eternal Father be your joy,4 St Michael the Archangel your guide. Ask him to watch over your actions so that they may be acceptable to the good God!

  5. Oh! dear daughter! if you knew how sweet the love of God is! It is the balm of our wounds amid the toils of this earth; it gives us strength to bear the sorrows we receive, and the beautiful trials become precious to us; in the end it sweetens suffering so that we grow hungry for it.5 Oh! sweet suffering! the world flees you because it does not know how to savour you.6

  6. You see, dear daughter, where I lose myself! When I enter this subject I would never stop; but duty obliges me to leave such sweet language and turn to other Institute matters, though I am not very well.

  7. So next week you will need to send Sr. A. Ludgarda and Sr. A. Ampelia to Pistoia; settle them well and give them plenty of advice; if Sr. A. [...]7 arrives from Genoa, send her to Lodi; if Sr. A. Coletta has arrived from [...], send her to Signora Maddalena at Cortemaggiore.8

  8. Today I expected letters from you, eager to know something about how the house is going and its finances. Two sacks will reach you, one of chestnuts and the other of chestnut flour, and they will also send you potatoes; if you need cheese write to me, and I promise to get it to you at once.

  9. I do not understand why no postulants have arrived yet; I left two at Lugo, but they are doing their postulancy there. Listen, write at once to Signora Ferrari about the hospital; tell her everything depends on her, that at least one be granted us.9 Insist; I have already written to papa.

  1. Tell Giuseppina10 I have received her letter and thank her. I would like to know whether she would prefer a little silk dress from Naples or a pair of coral earrings; let her tell me honestly without preambles or compliments, for I regard her as my own, so I must think about it. Or would she like something else?

  2. The Father greets you and thanks you for your letter. You see how long I have written? You must be tired of reading.

Goodbye, yours for ever,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The original is dated 12.3.80, but the first secretaries read 5 (May) instead of 3 and so filed it among that month's letters.

2 Obedience is the sure way, the only one, that makes us progress in love, since it sets us on the way of Christ, who from his entry into the world (Heb 10:5) to death on a cross (Phil 2:8) was obedience, that is, adherence to God through a series of intermediaries.

3 She moves from dialogue with her daughter to ardent prayer, rising with her to the one Good.

4 Love Jesus with ardent love and let yourself be carried like a child in the Father's arms. The Mother lives this intense relationship of love and teaches others to live it.

5 Becoming hungry for suffering: living Jesus' longing: "I came to bring fire to the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptised with, and what stress I am under until it is completed!" (Lk 12:49-50).

6 The world flees you, because it cannot gather the fruit of the cross, which is the fire of love, the gift of the Holy Spirit.

7 Sr. A. Maurina arrived from Genoa and Sr. A. Francesca took her to Lodi. Cf. L 50, n. 6.

8 Sr. A. Coletta arrived from Invorio. At Cortemaggiore, in the home-nursing community housed in the house donated by Signora Maddalena Parmigiani. Cf. L 51, n. 7.

9 Signora Ferrari of Genoa, who was to plead for the Daughters of Saint Anne to be taken on at a hospital. Cf. L 65, n. 2.

10 to Giuseppina, her sister. Cf. L 49, n. 2.

She asks for reduced fares for the Sisters' journeys as members of a charitable Institute.

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. The petitioner, being head of a charitable Institute devoted to nursing the sick at home and in hospitals, to Infant Schools for both sexes and to taking in poor abandoned girls, and having continually to send members to various cities of Italy where the Institute has houses, begs Your Excellency to obtain reduced fares in 2nd class carriages, as other Institutes like hers have already obtained.

Trusting in a kind and favourable reply, allow me to call myself Your Most Illustrious Excellency's

Most humble Sister Anna Maria

Rosa Gattorno, Superior General

of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne

1 It can be taken as written by M. Rosa in Florence during her visit. Sr. A. Santina Solenghi in fact informed her in Rome on 19.3.'80 that she had handed her letter to the Director General on 17.3 and would follow up the matter.

She explains how to answer the Priest who is presenting a postulant. Advice and encouragement.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have just read yours with the letters enclosed and am sending them back; answer that Father that from all the remarks the lady makes I find she is not called to our life, so she cannot be admitted. That is the answer you must give.1

  2. In a few days a postulant will come to you from Bagnacavallo and she is to bring F. 400. Perhaps she will be accompanied by another; I am not yet sure.

  3. Otherwise everything you have done is fine; take courage.

  4. Greet Giuseppina2 for me, and believe me yours; I am in a hurry; I have received the other one too. As for the one from Sestri, that is fine, I will write to her; meanwhile I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. For your information, tomorrow at 5 p.m. I leave for Pisa, God willing. Goodbye.

1 She returns the letters of a postulant and of the Father presenting her, and explains that she should not be accepted.

2 Giuseppina is her niece, sister of Sr. A. Francesca. She had no vocation but liked being at the Mother House. She was a witness at the ordinary process in Genoa. Cf. Positio, pp. 661-62.

She comforts her, advising her not to give weight to what the Sisters say. She gives her various tasks. Encouragement and expressions of gratitude, pleasure and affection.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. I received yours and hear of your distress, and I assure you it grieves me greatly.2 You tell me you would gladly come; well, be patient a little and I will do everything to please you, but the thought of that poor house left alone and abandoned truly pains me.

  2. Tell me, who dares to make you suffer? I really want to know, for I will certainly take steps and put it right!3 But! If it is Sr. A. Angelica!! Poor creature! She is not worth heeding. If it is Sr. A. Nazarena, even less! And I do not think there are any others. So?4

  3. Listen, write me everything clearly. Look, has Sr. A. Maurina arrived, and perhaps Sr. A. Coletta?5 If Sr. A. Maurina is over her fevers, take her to Lodi,6 where you can take Peppina as your companion for the return, and meanwhile see a little of what they do and say, and say something to Sr. A. Colomba so that she does not take so many liberties. I enclose a postal order for F. 100; have Francesco cash it.7 Keep your spirits up, for you will see that you will be happy.

  4. Dear daughter, your expressions of affection for me and for the Institute were extremely dear to me and I am...8 Oh! God bless you! Enough, in person. If you knew, dear daughter, how swamped I am with work, you would not believe it. I shall stay here until Wednesday; on Saturday,

God willing, I shall be in Rome, the eve of Palm Sunday.9

Goodbye in haste, yours, yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date — 14 rather than 24 — is clear from various elements of the text and from other letters of the Mother and Sr. A. Francesca's correspondence.

2 Dated the 14th; she refers to it at several points. "Melancholy has invaded my heart," her niece had confessed.

3 Another remark of Francesca's: "the few professed sisters always seem to speak mockingly".

4 She tries to dispel her impressions and at the same time helps her rise above them.

5 Sr. A. Coletta Faccini. Cf. L 51,6 n. 7.

6 She did go to Lodi on the 20th to accompany Sr. A. Maurina.

7 Cf. L 51,3.

8 "We shall make ourselves worthy to be called your daughters through holy obedience...", wrote Sr. A. Francesca.

9 She stayed until Wednesday 17th, then went via Montalto di Castro and reached Rome on the 20th, Holy Saturday.

She urges her to take care of herself and encourages her. She asks her to send a picture of Saint Anne, to advise a Sister and to guide the community in a life of perfect communion.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. Yesterday I wrote to you, and now again to tell you I have received yours2 and am delighted to hear you are better; for pity's sake take care of yourself, look after your health and remember you have many things to do, all for the glory of God! Courage then, for it is a time of work and suffering, to receive one day an eternal joy;3 so be cheerful.

  2. Now I would like you to send me the picture of Saint Anne, the one stuck to the inside of the door of the wardrobe, the big one holding the church things, the chasubles.4 Put a round stick inside, also wrapped, roll the saint round it, wrap her in a parcel and send her to this House; address it to: M. Biscioni, Parish Priest of S. Michele in Borgo, Pisa.

  3. Yesterday I sent you a letter there with a telegraphic money order for F. 100; have Francesco collect it. If you need anything write to me and I will send it at once.

  4. Now I will try to do all I can to meet your wishes and those of dear Beppina;5 I am sure it will be to come to Rome for a while, but if I do not manage it you must not put it down to my will, no, but! I too, as you know well, am bound; enough!

  5. Pray! God alone sees what and how many things I would like to do for you two, especially for you, my dear, for ever my dear daughter. God will do everything for our good, and rest assured that what I did with Sr. A. Ulderica was truly for the best, and you ! ! One day, in person, I am sure you will thank me and be extremely happy.6

6. If Sr. A. Coletta comes, scold her soundly and put her in community, forbidding her any kind of penance; those of the community alone must suffice.7 Make sure she does not stay with the novices and talk with their mistress — never to this novice mistress; I would not want her to own anything, but everything to be held in common, everything.8

I urge you to watch over perfect community life, and the food too. I hope you have received the vecchiette,9 which Giuseppa will like; we are now at the end of Lent. God willing, tomorrow at 6 a.m. I leave for Montalto. Goodbye, warm greetings, and I hold you close in the heart of Jesus, where I am

your affectionate M. Sr. A. Rosa

1 The date is derived from two letters of Sr. A. Francesca to M. Rosa: 15.3.1880 and 18.3.1880.

2 Dated 15 March.

3 It is a time of work and suffering. Following Christ in self-giving to others involves being conformed to His "suffering". Cf. Lk 24:26; 1 Pet 4:1.

4 Now I would like... the chasubles. The picture of Saint Anne had been placed on the inside door of the large cupboard where the chasubles and other church furnishings were kept.

5 Beppina is Sr. A. Francesca's sister. Cf. L 49, n. 2.

6 Sr. A. Ulderica Tazioli had been transferred to Ferrara. Cf. L 45. Sr. A. Francesca, who was fond of her, suffered from this, but later realised that her removal "had been good for the whole" running of the community. Cf. L Francesca S. to M. Rosa: 15.3.1880.

7 Sr. A. Coletta Faccini. Scold her: warn her not to do penances beyond those of the community.

8 This refers to the novice mistress, as Sr. A. Francesca writes on 18 March.

9 The vecchiette, some local delicacy.

She explains how to answer the Inspector about the statistics of the young women living at the Mother House.

A.M.E

Dear daughter,

  1. You will receive this letter from Sr. A.'s hands; I would like to tell you so many things, but I am writing while people are talking.2

  2. Listen, answer the Inspector that we have no boarders,3 but that we give the statistics every year; besides, we cannot run a school because we do not want one.4 But listen, answer only this: that we have no boarders, there is only ourselves, and every year the statistics are given to the Town Council.5 If he wants them we will send them; you must not put down sisters or postulants, only the baptismal name, nothing more.

  3. God willing, I shall be in Rome on Wednesday evening.6 Tomorrow at 11 I leave for Montalto, for your information.

Your affectionate M. R.

Greetings to all; and how is the Father?

1 This letter was written on the same day as the previous one, as the repeated news of her departure for Montalto shows.

2 ... but I am writing while people near me are talking; so she cannot linger over writing.

3 There were no boarders at the Mother House, only postulants and novices, who did not attend ordinary courses of study.

4 They were being prepared for religious life, not to obtain school qualifications.

5 The statistics on the numbers in the house were sent annually.

6 Cf. L 50, n. 9.

Brief notes about a house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am writing to you again; meanwhile I enclose a bill from Pennabilli;2 tell Onorata that the teacher is no longer needed;3 for now we hope to have settled everything; so greetings to you all, and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

A.M.E

Dear daughter,

  1. I always find you fearful; why? You know how much I love you and how I am towards you; so away with all fears, leave everything as it is and think only of getting well,2 and as soon as you can travel I want you here with me for a while; it will take your mind off things and you will be strong and robust again.

  2. Write and set my mind at rest. Be cheerful, you know? Try to eat well and drink good wine and meat broth, and you will soon recover. A big hug in my dear Crucified One,

affectionate M. Rosa

She tells her to send two Sisters at once and asks for news.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. Send me Sr. A. [...] and Sr. A. [»..]1 at once. I have no letters and am extremely anxious. I am unwell, with such a headache! but patience!

  2. Write to me, send me the sisters and tell me whether you received the letters with the money order inside.

Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

My daughter,

  1. You are quite right to say I do not write to you, but if I have someone else write you mind it, and so we must be patient!2 I am, I can say, overwhelmed with work.

  2. Now I tell you I approve all you have done3 and the troubles you had to endure. Oh! unfortunately they make a mess of things and then we have to suffer for it.4 My God!

  3. Be patient; Jesus will help you and give you courage to bear it patiently.

  4. Here are 87 Francs from the Prefecture for the girls, for the quarter now due to you.5

Goodbye, yours for all ages,

affectionate M. Rosa

You are F. 2 short, which the Province itself kept; I will tell you the reason in person.

My daughter,

1. Just one line, because I have a headache and I assure you I am tied up with business.1 I return the signed paper; yes, well done, I am pleased with all you have done; be content and try to obtain these travel privileges.2 Enough.

Goodbye; greetings to dear Sr. A. Eletta and to you, and I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear of your troubles and am truly sorry. Be careful when they portonano (?) you, and pay no heed to anyone, for pity's sake; do you understand?1 With this headache I cannot write at length.
  1. Read them these two lines:2

Listen, your behaviour grieves me greatly. Oh! stop it, or I shall have to take firm measures. Oh! what a sorrow! amid so many troubles!

3. Do not be upset if I do not write; I am overwhelmed with work.

Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Troubles... understand! Above all the disrespectful behaviour of two Sisters who, among other things, side with the girls and grumble when the Superior rebukes them.

In Rome too she has found poverty because of the general economic crisis. She urges them to be thrifty. She has met her grandson Carlino.

My son,

  1. I find your letter a little agitated and, as usual, it is all prompted by a bit of envy, isn't it?1 Last night I received the telegram, which was very dear to me; so God be blessed! Here nothing reigns but mourning and poverty; there is nothing to hope for.2

  2. Yesterday I saw your sister-in-law and brother; they are very well; I see everyone's pockets are ailing, poor things!!!3 So it is no wonder the Daughters of Saint Anne are beyond poverty. Ah! What poverty all along the line!!!

  3. Be thrifty! You complain, but! Others see you as very fortunate! So? Are you convinced?4 Rome! What an effect it had on me! Ah! a dreadful melancholy, who knows!5 Carlino is far from resembling Nonny and Nonetto. Oh! what a difference!! like night and day!!6 Tell Carla not to worry, there is no danger of jealousy!! You will hear in person! che bolettaWV

Greetings to you both and kisses to the little girls, while I call myself your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 In his L of 21.3.'80 Gaspare complained of the behaviour towards them of Carlotta's cousin, Sr. A. Francesca Savignone, and concluded: "... I realise I am not wrong when I judge someone, and I shall keep her at a distance".

2 She alludes to the rich nobility, who kept up appearances with their usual life of luxury but in reality had to reckon with the general situation, so that she could not hope for financial help from them (there is nothing to hope for).

My daughter,

  1. Having a minute: listen, that lay woman is really your disgrace.1 Do you know what they say in town? That the lay teacher is the one who teaches and the Daughters of Saint Anne are ignorant and so make use of her. Do you see what a fine honour? Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

My daughter,

your affectionate M. Rosa

My daughter,

My daughter,

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I gather from your letter that Sr. A. Florinda told you a fine lie, or rather a distortion, for this is how it went.1 The Father came and said to me: "Where are the account books?" I answered: "We cannot see them, because the Superior, with my permission, has taken the keys, and unless there is one that fits I cannot get them".2 I asked Sr. A. Florinda whether she had any keys and tried them, but none fitted; so I wanted to see her face, and I said: "I did not think to have them left with me".3

  2. So you see how they twist things and then embroider them? Ah! what a world! Likewise if we urged economy, it is because when you are not there one must always be wary, knowing whom one is dealing with!4 So there is no need to think of bringing or sending the books!

  4. How are you? Perhaps, who knows, I may come back your way instead of taking the road to Foggia. Everyone tells me it will be too hot and I shall not stand it. Enough, it is still a long way off! for I have a great deal of work!6
