3 She did leave on 6 April.

Let her take care to balance service to the sick with observance and the Sisters' real capacities. News and advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you are doing a great many night watches; this displeases me, and I tell you I do not want it, for if you sit up nights, I tell you, you cannot and I do not want it; so you will always be at home and able to supervise.2

  2. And then, how can observance be kept? This first, and then you will have everything, if observance is in your House.3

  3. The world was made little by little, and when the sick cannot be accepted they are not accepted, for it is better to send them away than to do more than your strength allows.4

  4. Tell the relatives of that Sister of ours to be patient; I will let them see her this summer, for now it is impossible; this summer they will give the money and I will have her accompanied, but not now.5

  5. So accept the postulant and put her in the kitchen, and you will see she will do well. At the end of April I will have two more sent to you, so they will be useful; for now a little patience is needed!

  6. Be cheerful and strong in health, and let us try to do everything for Jesus. Greetings to all the sisters; God bless them all; and I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 She had written (L n.d.): "I go on night watch two or three times a week... I go collecting alms...".

3 The Superior's primary task is the smooth running and spiritual growth of the community.

4 A very wise rule.

5 The relatives of Sr. A. Ermanna Fantozzi.

She is tired, has much work and longs to return.

Dearest children,

1. Sr. A. Benedetta is handing me the letter so that I can add a couple of lines. What shall I tell you? That I am very tired; so much work! Dear children, you long for me, but I long to return. I am always trying to get things done quickly; I always put everything aside for the dear little girls.1

Goodbye. Affectionate greetings, and I am

Your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She keeps the presents she receives for her dear little granddaughters Maria Adelaide and Rosetta.

Directions and advice about a novice, the postulants and the running of the house.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. I hear all you tell me about Sr. A. Serafina, all of it; so take Sr. A. Serafina out of the novitiate and from under the obedience of that unfortunate woman. Oh! what a hard character!1

  2. Checco is going to Alessandria for his examinations. Let us hope all goes well; I have just sent mamma a letter I received from Rome; I assure you one could not wish for more!2

  3. If the postulant arrives with 2000, do not spend it; first we must see whether she stays, for it would be a problem.3 Listen, I return the postulant's letter; accept her. I hope you have already accepted the teacher; we need her.

  4. You did well to bake bread at home; it will be a saving. Find out the price of wheat; ask Count Camillo and then write to me, and we will buy a little,4 but only a little, for it keeps falling and, thank God, we shall have a fine harvest!

I end because I am really in a hurry; I am yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 There was friction between the over-strict mistress and a novice.

2 Cf. L 78,4; 81,1.

3 The sum the postulant brought for her keep before clothing must not be committed; it is best to await her decision to stay or go home, in which case the money had to be returned.

4 Ask Count Camillo Marazzani the current price of wheat.

She thanks her for the prayers. She is better. She asks for news of the Sisters sent to her community. All she has done is good.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Thanks to your prayers I am on my feet and can do my duty well enough. Thank you, then! My head is not tormenting me, so I can write with less effort.

  2. Now to practical matters: the sisters have arrived; are they useful to you? are they doing well? watch their tongues!1 Otherwise all is well.

  3. Courage; if you think you should go to Pisa, go and please Angiolina.2 As for the postulants, all is well; I will do my best to pass through Pistoia.3 Be cheerful and believe me, in haste,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Pay attention to what they say.

2 Angiolina, Canon Biagini's servant, had expressed a wish "to see the Pisa house". Cf. L Crocifissa Fiocchi: 8.4.80 to M. Rosa.

3 On her journey back to Piacenza.

She has done everything well in accepting the postulants and she approves it all. On her return they will meet in Piacenza, have no doubt.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Your letter, which I have just finished reading:1 I see you always fear you are not doing well; put that fear aside and act with confidence! Well done! Courage! Everything done well about the postulants; I approve it all.

  2. As for your not being there when I arrive, will you be? for, in all confidence and secrecy, I shall not be able to be in Piacenza before early June, God willing, so that I can work continuously as I did, without interruption.

  3. So, about the Sisters to be sent, I did not quite understand; do what you think best, but at once, for at Lodi they need them badly.3

Goodbye, in haste

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Dated 9 April 1880.

2 At the end of April Sr. A. Francesca was to go to Arena Po to help the Superior draw up the balance sheet.

3 The nursing Sister had fallen ill and needed replacing.

She explains how to proceed to collect an inheritance. Let her wait for a copy of the will.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear from your letter of the inheritance you have received, but I do not want you to give anyone power of attorney;1 go to Genoa, see that you leave nothing to anyone and take good advice;2 before signing I would like you to send me a copy of the will, so that I can tell you what to do.

  2. Say that you can do nothing, because, as the goods are not yours,3 you cannot dispose of anything given your vow, and before signing and deciding you are bound, under penalty, to refer to the Mother;4 and moreover that these goods were left with the intention of serving the Community.

  3. So set off and send me a copy of the will at once, and then I will reply, for I can also use the telegraph. On my way back from Rome I am coming to Florence, because I need to stop at Pistoia. For your information I shall be there in early June.

Goodbye; greetings to all, and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 In her L of 10.4.'80 she had told her that Fr Antonio Accinelli had informed her of the death of "that Priest who had left her his heir" and asked her to send him power of attorney.

2 Leave nothing of the inheritance, and seek advice so as to act rightly.

3 As the goods are not yours. The testator had made the Superior his heir as representative of the community.

4 By the vow of poverty you are bound (under penalty) to refer to the Mother for the necessary permissions.

She fears letters are going astray. She is pleased with the good news of the Sisters. Let her not worry about the Sunday Masses; she will settle it on her return. She will bring a postulant with her.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. I gather from your little note received yesterday2 that you are without our letters; can it be? when I wrote a few hours before leaving and then as soon as I arrived. Can they be going astray?

  2. I would like to know whether Onorata has received my letter, because, seeing no reply to the many things I asked her — indeed two letters, one from Rome and the other from here — I am worried they are going astray. Now I shall not write for 3 days, as I am going to Giugliano and will be back on Friday.3

  3. You ask about the Sisters who want to go to the Bishop with the postulant: take them yourself and do not leave them; a brief visit and then away; greet him for me.4 I assure you the good news of the Sisters is a great consolation to me.

  4. I am sending this letter back to you; accept the two postulants on the terms stated in it.

  5. As for the Sunday Masses, tell the Chaplain that when I arrive I will settle them myself, for the story is too long to tell!5

  6. I hope you will put a chain on Beppina and not let her go away;6 for pity's sake let her wait for me; I will come with a dear little Countess who will later become a nun; she is already with me.

In 20 days a beautiful piano will reach you, but you must not give away the one there, no; the one arriving belongs to this girl, who plays

very well. Tell Carla, so she will be pleased, and Beppa. Goodbye, I am overwhelmed with work! Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

My head always aches!

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Francesca's letter it answers and from the context.

2 The note is dated 10 April 1880.

3 A house had been opened at Giugliano di Campania.

4 A postulant had been given "an errand", probably by her Bishop.

5 The story is too long to explain, and there was no urgency.

6 Beppina (Giuseppina) was at the Mother House but had no vocation. Cf. L 49, n. 2.

Advice about a Sister and the house.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. From the telegram you will have seen I did not want you to send Sr. A. Natalina.2 "My God! Do not trust her; keep her well watched, for she will stir up gossip, and I want to know always how she behaves, both she and the other, for otherwise painful steps will have to be taken; do you understand me?

  2. You must not leave them long in those cloisters;3 try to change them, and I hope you went with them yourself.

  3. Otherwise everything you have done is fine; if the two Sisters have arrived, you can also use these two to relieve the other two after 10 or 8 days;4 not longer, I think, for I have tried others already, and they soon get used to that very monotonous life.

  4. So be careful; I enclose a line for Sr. A. Liberata, which you will give her. Goodbye; greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is inferred from the related correspondence of Superior Sr. A. Guglielma, who announced the departure, and of Sup. Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, who reported the arrival by L of 16.4.1880.

2 The Sister had already left. Cf. L 79, n. 2.1 The expressions are not clear.

4 The two Sisters who had arrived could replace the others after 8-10 days.

She forbids her to do night watches with the sick. She asks for reports on the Pisa house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. In a spare moment I answer yours, which I received yesterday in Naples.1 I hear you are doing night watches; I absolutely do not want it, for you no longer have the strength for such exertion.

  2. How can you tell me you left the poor Canon alone? Oh! That is too much; what if he were taken ill? No, no, such things will not do; they are imprudent.2

  3. So you tell me you are 14 — how so? You must be fifteen, surely?3 Enough; this letter will find you already back from Pisa, so you can write and tell me how that house is going.

I shall be there in early June. Greetings to all, and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa. Tomorrow I shall be in Naples.

1 She had written on 12 April.

2 As there were many sick to nurse, she too, with Canon Biagini's servant, had done night duty, leaving the canon alone in the house. The Mother disapproves.

3 She knows, on the contrary, that they are 15.

She has much work and is unwell. She asks her to go to Pisa for two days.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am so overwhelmed with work that I do not know how to manage it all; besides, my headache torments me and I assure you I cannot [...] Enough!1

  2. You should go to Pisa for at least two days; I assure you it is my wish,2 and then straight back to Pistoia. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She breaks off the sentence with: enough.

2 She had been told that Sr. A. Crocifissa's presence was needed, since she had founded and started the house and continued to follow its progress. Cf. L 25; 30; 38; 103.

■

Permission to go collecting alms.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just one line; be patient, for when I come I will settle everything! When you have to go collecting alms,1 take whomever you think best; I have no time to answer everything, as I am immensely busy.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 40,1; 83,1; 109,1.

Let her not accept the postulant of "advanced age"; the others, yes.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. In great haste, for I am overwhelmed with work. Listen, the old postulant you mention cannot be accepted, no, because of her age;1 otherwise all is well; the other young ones, yes.

  2. The Father who succeeded Father Olivieri — you can tell Marchioness Anguissola, for she knows him, since she gives him alms.2

Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Francesca had described her as "already of advanced age". Cf. L to M. Rosa: 15.4.1880.

2 In the same L she said that Fr Alessandro had brought a "visiting friar" to see the Sisters. The Mother alludes to the latter; she knows him, and so does Marchioness Fanny Anguissola.

She has asked the Holy Father's blessing for him and his brother. She has received the other birth certificate and will send it.

Most worthy Count,

  1. I have not written again because I kept waiting for the certificates of the two, so as to tell you everything at once.1

  2. So first I will tell you that I received from the Holy Father a special blessing for you and your brother;2 he received me kindly and in his goodness had me sit down. How good he is! to me, so wretched and unworthy a creature!

  3. Now in Naples I am in a sea of business, but always thinking of you and eager for news of you and your eyes. Sr. A. Battistina has shown me a keen wish to know how you are, and the day before yesterday, when I was with her,3 we often exclaimed: "Oh! If the Counts were here, how they would enjoy themselves! Come! Come!

  4. Yesterday at last I received another certificate. You will see that this one too has the father, or the mother, living, but rest assured they can do no harm, for they would sooner benefit than diminish or appropriate; then it is enough to say that he is the Father's brother, and I think that suffices.4

  5. I will send you the other later, because there was a mistake and the one I have is not right.5 My God! What it takes to get anything from town councils! Write and tell me how you are, or have someone write.

Greet your brother, Father Cirillo and Don Luigi. Believe me ever

your affectionate Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

1 On 26 March of that year the Count had written to tell her he had received the birth certificate of Marchioness Carrega (Sr. A. Benedetta).

2 His brother, Count Maurizio, was unwell.

3 when I was with her. She had gone to Giugliano di Campania. Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi had nursed Countess Isabella Caracciolo. Cf. L to M. Rosa: 20.4.'80 from Francesco Caracciolo.

4 another certificate... suffices. She has received the birth certificate of Sr. A. Vincenza Tornatore, whose parents are living, but that can do no harm; indeed it is an advantage. It is enough to say that the Sister's father is Fr Tornatore's brother.

3 She will send the other birth certificate later, because there is an error in how it was filled in.

She explains how to deal with two Sisters who will arrive at the Mother House.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. A line in haste. Listen, at Arena Po a sister has fallen ill and they need another. See whether you have one to send;1 you could take her yourself, couldn't you? so as not to let her go alone, since you are going anyway.2

  2. Listen, Sr. A. Matilde will come to you; treat her well;3 tell her I will soon have her study; then, with kindness, you will rid her of all the crooked ideas she has, and she will get back on the right path. Take great care that she does not write to her sister secretly, I beg you.

  3. Listen, Sr. A. Salvatore will come to you; send her straight on to Pistoia, where she will find my orders as to where she must go; for pity's sake send her as soon as she arrives. If money has come, give her about 100.4 And as soon as you can, give Gaspare 300 for the interest he has to pay.

  4. I hope postulants have arrived; tell me how many there are and whether you expect more.5

Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

1 See if you can choose one as a replacement.

2 She herself was due to go to Arena Po at the end of the month. Cf. L 88, n. 2.

3 Sr. A. Matilde Arnedos. She was unsure of her vocation.

4 Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi. The Mother asked Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi to send her on to Palermo with other Sisters. The money (£ 100) was for the journey. Cf. L 100,3.

5 There were 14 postulants; she was expecting more.

She may accept the postulant. Advice about her sister Giuseppina. She asks for the printed form of the Clothing rite.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. Tell the postulant you will receive her with the extra 200.1 Send Sr. A. Nazzarena at once to Lodi, where they need a cook.2

  2. As for Giuseppina, if she comes with the Marchioness, remember it is very hot here and dress her modestly;3 not one of the hats she has, no, you know, modest ones like caps of that sort, for here you see nothing else. If she needs anything, buy it without saying a word; get her what she needs to be modest. Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

3. Send me one of the sheets used [for] the clothing ceremony;^4^they are in the last pigeonhole where the newspapers are, the same as the one you know is used for clothing!

1 ... the extra 200. Over 200 francs, 250 to be exact, Sr. A. Francesca had written.

2 Sr. A. Nazzarena Pastorini had told Sr. A. Francesca she wished to be transferred.

3 The Mother explains to Sr. A. Francesca the kind of modest clothing her sister should wear.

4 The clothing of 4 postulants took place on 29 April in Naples.

She has received her letters. She reminds her to put into practice the advice given before her departure. She encourages her and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received the two letters; in one I found a little fear and heard of you at Pistoia;1 in the other I see you are happier and no longer so fearful, and likewise about the good Parish Priest.2

  2. For pity's sake do not forget to put into practice the advice I gave you before leaving; what can I do? I am always wary of writing, because...

  3. So courage, we shall soon see each other.3 Pray and have others pray; tell the dear Sisters. I should also tell you that I shall not be back before mid-June, so there is time.

Goodbye; greetings to all, and a thousand good wishes to you in the Heart of Jesus; I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 She had gone to Pistoia to ask Superior Crocifissa's advice.

2 In the other, of 21 April, she seems more sure of herself. The parish priest gives her good advice for the work.

3 Soon... though two months remain, as she specifies just afterwards.

Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi will come to Pistoia to collect three Sisters. If possible let her pay their journey to Naples, or at least to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear from your letter that you have not gone to Pisa; if you think you should go, I leave you free.1

  2. Now pay attention: Sr. A. Salvatore will come; give her Sr. A. Norberta and both of those who came from Piacenza, the latest ones though;2 remember they must do night watches and are needed for Naples. For pity's sake do not send me old ones, no; I always mean novices, and Sr. A. Norberta; do you understand?3

  3. For pity's sake I beg you; only, if you could give them the money to get here, you would do me a great favour; I have written to the Superior of Piacenza to give £ 700 if she had it, but fearing she may not, if you could, she will repay you as soon as she has it, for they are needed to open a House in Palermo, and they are to give me the travel money.4

  4. So see what you can do; if you cannot, telegraph me and tell me what you are doing, whether you can give them at least as far as Rome, and from there I will try to turn to Brother Agostino.5 If you do not have the 100 [f.], you can give them the fare to Rome.

  5. We will do this: give the enclosed to Sr. A. Salvatore. Goodbye, thank you for the prayers; thank the Sisters for me and give them my love; and you receive a big6

affection from your M. R.

1 The Superior had not gone to Pisa, since the Superior of that community had come to her for explanations and advice. Cf. L Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi: 16.4.'80, to M. Rosa.

2 Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi was about to leave for Palermo to open a house. The latest novices: Sr. A. Settimia and Sr. A. Restilde. Cf. idem. 5 Old ones means in vocation, not in age.

4 Travel expenses were generally borne by the local authorities' administrations.

5 Brother Agostino Donadio.

6 She left it unfinished.

She asks her to submit the application for reduced fares on the Southern Railways.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. The day before yesterday I learnt that the Sisters of St Vincent had the good fortune to obtain half-price tickets on the Southern line,1 and what about us? See what you can do; go and enquire, with that fine opportunity you have;2 do not delay; they tell me one must apply to the Ministry.

  2. Listen: if the Superior is not there, you do it, dear Eletta; send for that gentleman.3 Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 57; 58; 63.

2 Director General Borgnini had expressed a favourable opinion.

3 The Superior had gone to Genoa. Cf. L 89,3. You do it. The Mother had addressed the letter to Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi.

// Fr Tornatore has invited Marchioness Anguissola to Naples. Let her go to her to hear her instructions and wishes.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. It is late and I am tired, but I must write all the same; so, in strict secrecy: the Father has written to the Marchioness to come to Naples and to take Giuseppina as her companion.1 So you can go to her and say: the Father (says) sent word that I should come to you to receive your orders and do as you tell me, including about the companion for Naples; and nothing more.2 See whether she says yes; then be sure to give Giuseppina some money so that she can buy anything she needs for the journey; I think they will stop in Florence and Rome; give them food.3 She pays for the whole journey; I mean the Marchioness pays for both.

1. Another worry! as if I did not have enough!4 My God! Let us leave that! Do you know anything about Checco?5

Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Fr Tornatore had invited Marchioness Fanny Anguissola to come to Naples accompanied by Giuseppina Savignone. Cf. L 75, n. 4; 98,2.

2 ... and nothing more: she was not to add other details.

3 give them food: prepare what they need to eat on the journey.

4 Another worry. The Marchioness's presence would bring her concerns.

5 Cf. L 86,2.

She is pleased with her service at Pisa. She will return at the end of the month. Advice. News of her own health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear many things about Pisa. Well done, my dear little lamb!1 I also received your telegram.

  2. You should have taken all the money from the one at Pisa.2 Listen, you can go back on the last day of the month, or for the opening of the Chapel3 I want you to be there; you understand, don't you?

  3. Listen, I have written a million times to that Superior4 to accept the postulant and put her in the kitchen, so she will be useful, won't she? You will do it when you go back, collecting the dowry and keeping it with you.

  4. So one thing I urge you: look after your health and do not eat strofugi.5 Goodbye, I am so busy and tired that my poor head...! pray for me and believe me yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

1 She had written on 21.4 with a report. She had gone there in response to the Mother's wish, and the Mother praises her docility. Cf. L 93,2; 100,1.

2 The Pisa superior had not kept the accounts, so Sr. A. Crocifissa had filled in the books for her and found a surplus of £ 300.

3 The Chapel was to be solemnly inaugurated on 1 May.

4 To the superior Antonietta Gallinari.

5 strofugi: a Genoese dialect expression.

The two Sisters should sit their certificate examinations at Ravenna. She will send the documents the Sister teacher is waiting for.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Your letter was a real consolation.1 Well done, well done! So tell them they will sit the examinations at Ravenna. Yes, Ravenna will be much better.2

  2. Thank the confessor for me, and a thousand blessings to you.3 Tell Sr. A. Leopoldina that I have written again about her certificate and hope to have everything.4

Goodbye, yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. Tell Sr. A. Leopoldina that I will tell her everything in person and she will be pleased.

1 She had reported the two sisters' success in their practice-teaching examinations.

2 Ravenna had been recommended by the Education Officer who had examined them.

3 The Confessor willingly gave the Sisters lessons.

4 Sr. A. Leopoldina Farina was waiting for the documents, including her qualification, to hand them to the school authorities.

Communications and advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Keep knocking again and again about the seats; do not let them sleep on it.1 I return the will;2 you did everything well, well done! As for the Sisters, we shall see when I come! Stand firm about the confessors. Goodbye,

your M. Rosa

About the seats: about railway ticket discounts. Cf. L 101,1. Cf. L 89,3.

Directions on accepting two postulants and on the community. News.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. A line in reply to yours, which I read last night on getting back from Capua at 9,1 and I hear you are afraid you did wrong. No, I tell you that you did everything very well.

  2. So I return the letters; one is not accepted; to the other, the one with a thousand F., reply that you cannot accept her unless she pays at least £ 500 and guarantees a franc a day for her stay, otherwise she should stay at home; the other 500 she will give at profession.

  3. The cobbler Sister,2 for pity's sake do not send her anywhere; indeed, see that she does not do night watches, so we shall have a good cobbler. Do not send anyone there, for Sr. A. Riparata will be well;3 do not worry about the cook; no one is indispensable in God's works!4 Write to me always. On Thursday there is a clothing of 4 here, and others remain whom I will bring when I come. Goodbye. In haste, yours always

affectionate M. Rosa

1 At S. Maria Capua Vetere the FSA worked in the hospital.

2 Sr. A. Altaria Amico was useful to the large community.

3 Sr. A. Riparata, who was to have been replaced at Arena Po, had recovered.

4 The cook, Sr. A. Nazzarena, was to leave the Mother House for Lodi. Sr. A. Francesca said she was worried about this. Cf. L 98,1.

She is astonished at the Superior's behaviour. Let her instruct her well. Advice and rules for accepting postulants.

A.M.R

My daughter,

  1. Oh! what misguided humility that thoughtless Superior has! What do you say? I assure you I am truly flabbergasted;1 please go for the opening of the house, that is, of the Chapel.2

  2. I hope that by the time you receive this letter the Sisters will have passed through, that is, been sent off.3

  3. So you can go back to Pisa and try to shake that Superior up; tell her this is misguided humility; do all you can to rouse her.4

  4. Listen, as for the postulant, accept her; you could put her in the kitchen if you think fit, otherwise send her to Piacenza, together with the one you accepted.

  5. Listen, those two you tell me about, from the missionary, I am very wary, for they have never given us a good one, and as an excuse they say they do not accept them without a dowry, which is not true at all, for they take poor girls just as we do and worse; but if they have faults, they send them to us!5 See them first, observe them well, make sure they are of legitimate parents, and so step by step, and if you then think them suitable, accept them,6 and send them along with the one from Pisa.

  6. For a cook, see whether you have one; you could take her there. Goodbye, yours for all ages,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 On 23.4 Sup. Crocifissa had written that Sup. Antonietta cannot assert herself and leaves the Sisters too free. Out of misguided humility she will not hear reports of their conduct with the sick, thinking them more capable than herself.

2 For the inauguration of the Chapel. Cf. L 103, n. 3.

3 Cf. L 100,2.

4 Do all you can: persuade her to act with awareness of her task as Superior and according to the Rules.

5 Listen, those... to us. She is doubtful about the two postulants presented by a missionary of the Alberoni College in Piacenza, and explains why: they have never given us a good one, using the excuse that they (the Daughters of Charity) cannot accept girls without a dowry, whereas in fact they too accept poor girls, but if they have faults they send them to us.

6 In any case examine them carefully, and if they meet the requirements, accept them.

She encloses the two letters sent to her for review. She is glad the postulants will increase.

A.M.E

My daughter,

  1. Here I am writing again; I forgot to put the two letters in.1
